newsitem.title: USA: U.S. High Court rejects Alabama sheriff liability.
newsitem.headline: U.S. High Court rejects Alabama sheriff liability.

text.p: A divided Supreme Court ruled Monday that sheriffs executing their law enforcement duties represent the state and cannot be held liable for alleged violations by local governments of constitutional rights.

The high court held by a 5-4 vote that sheriffs in Alabama represent the state, not their counties, and thus cannot be considered a final policymaker for the local government alleged to have committed the violations.

In a related development, the justices agreed to decide the legal standard to be used for liability in police pursuit cases and whether an officer should be entitled to partial immunity from lawsuits seeking damages.

The court will consider whether plaintiffs in such lawsuits alleging violations of constitutional rights must show the police conduct "shocks the conscience" or meet the less stringent standard of showing "reckless disregard and "deliberate indifference" for someone's safety.

The justices will hear arguments in the case from Sacramento, Calif., during their term that begins in October, with a ruling expected early next year. The suit was brought on behalf of the family of a 16-year-old boy, a passenger on a motorcycle who died after a high-speed chase because the police officer saw the driver commit traffic law violations.

The Alabama ruling was a defeat for Walter McMillian, who had been convicted of murder and spent nearly six years on death row in Alabama. His conviction was overturned because local officials withheld key evidence proving his innocence.
He then filed a civil lawsuit against government officials involved in his arrest and imprisonment including the sheriff in Monroe County where he had been named as a defendant.

A federal judge dismissed the suit, ruling the county could not be held liable for the sheriff's actions because sheriffs were not final policymakers for the county in the area of law enforcement. A U.S. appeals court upheld the decision.
Chief Justice William Rehnquist said for the Supreme Court majority the lower courts were correct in dismissing the case.
The ruling also was a defeat for the Justice Department, which had argued that under Alabama kaw the county sheriff exercises final policymaking authority for law enforcement.

The court's four most liberal members dissented from the ruling, calling it "misguided," but they described it as a narrow decision and predicted it will have little impact on county liability in most jurisdictions.

Also Monday, the high court rejected a constitutional challenge to a Louisiana law that provides for a possible death penalty for those who rape children under age 12. The case involved Patrick Bethley, who has AIDS. He is accused of raping his young daughter and two stepdaughters.

Justice John Paul Stevens in a brief statement joined by two other justices said the court's action "does not in any sense constitute a ruling on the merits of the case." He noted Bethley has "been neither convicted nor sentenced for any crime," a step usually required before the Supreme Court will agree to hear a case.
